article.summary: ContextDB is an embedded Rust database substrate for agentic-memory applications. It combines relational rows, bounded graph traversal, and exact vector search under transactional storage and policy constraints, while leaving the memory schema and agent-level selection logic to the application. This is a source review; no runtime or benchmark results were collected.

who_what.text: The official project describes ContextDB as an embedded Rust database for agentic-memory applications, combining relational rows, bounded graph traversal, and vector similarity in one transactional store. It supplies storage and policy primitives rather than a prescribed memory schema or agent-facing memory model.

The roster position is 147: ContextDB, slug contextdb, listed repository https://github.com/context-graph-ai/contextdb, with repository_status explicit. The pinned Atlas record is retained only for identity and locator attribution, not as assessment evidence.

architecture.text: The README and architecture guide describe a Rust workspace with a relational row store as canonical data, secondary graph adjacency and vector structures, SQL parsing/planning, an engine, and CLI and sync-server crates. A single-file embedded store uses MVCC snapshots to coordinate relational, graph, and vector state in transactions; the schema is supplied by the application.

Graph queries use bounded breadth-first traversal with edge-type and direction controls. Vector columns support cosine distance and exact search; the current docs say indexed search is unavailable and the clustered index is disabled. These facilities do not imply built-in embeddings or a memory-specific data model.

The engine source and architecture guide describe a single writer per database file, concurrent readers, and scoped read sessions. The relational source is authoritative while graph and vector indexes are derived structures.

behavior.text: Write: callers define tables and constraints, then use SQL INSERT, UPDATE, upsert, and DELETE or the Rust API. Transactions accumulate mutations in a write set and publish relational, graph, and vector changes atomically; schema constraints such as IMMUTABLE, STATE MACHINE, DAG, foreign keys, and PROPAGATE are enforced by the engine.

Update and correction: ordinary UPDATE/upsert is available subject to constraints. An IMMUTABLE column cannot be rewritten; the query guide illustrates correction by inserting a new row and marking the prior row superseded. HISTORY ALL retains superseded versions by default; HISTORY CURRENT ONLY permits maintenance to reclaim older versions, and does not restore history once removed.

Delete and retention: SQL DELETE and DROP TABLE are supported. RETAIN can expire rows; maintenance and MVCC reader snapshots affect when old versions and physical pages can be reclaimed. The documentation distinguishes logical visibility/removal from file shrinkage and does not promise forensic erasure or removal from operator-held backups. Sync custody describes an all-or-nothing fleet erasure boundary for its governed units.

Retrieval: SQL selects and bounded graph traversals can filter and order rows; vector columns support exact cosine-distance search and result limits. Scoped handles can constrain rows by context, scope label, and optional ACL principal. The CLI has bounded reads with refusal rather than silent truncation; the embedded execute API has a distinct uncapped contract. ContextDB itself does not select or generate agent memories.

Scope isolation: the database has no general multi-tenant orchestration. Context/scope/ACL constraints are opt-in application declarations and handle settings; authorization behavior differs for live owner-scoped handles and direct reads of a closed store, where file permissions govern access. The capability index says --tenant-id is a sync namespace whose members replicate together, not a tenant-isolation boundary.

Provenance and evidence: there is no built-in epistemic memory provenance or claim-evidence model. Applications can use immutable columns, state transitions, history, event/custody manifests, and sync receipts to preserve declared records and delivery history. Those mechanisms record database state or transport custody; they do not verify the truth of an agent-generated claim.

Efficiency and observability: MVCC separates readers from serialized writers; architecture documents bounded work/memory accounting, paged reads, maintenance, snapshots, and exact vector search. The engine exposes subscriptions, plugin lifecycle/query hooks, tracing warnings for guarded contention, and finite read/cursor budgets in supported surfaces. These are design and instrumentation descriptions, not measured latency, cost, or storage-efficiency results.

metrics.evidence: The database exposes SQL, graph and exact vector retrieval but no agent-level memory policy; no quality or abstention workload was run.
Update, state-machine, immutable-column, and history policies are documented; no correction sequence was executed.
Logical deletion, retention, MVCC cleanup, and sync erasure boundaries are documented; no post-delete retrieval or residual-copy check was run.
Context, scope, ACL, and sync namespaces are documented as separate mechanisms; no cross-scope or cross-tenant isolation workload was run.
No built-in claim-support or citation-verification layer was identified; no adjudication workload was run.
Bounded reads and exact vector search are source-visible; no latency workload was run.
Transactional writes, maintenance, and synchronization are documented; no acknowledgment-to-recall timing was measured.
ContextDB is a database substrate and this review collected no model-token or provider-cost data.
The architecture describes page storage, retention, history cleanup, and compaction behavior; no corpus-attributable storage measurement was made.

limits.text: ContextDB is a storage engine with no built-in schema, embeddings model, agent integration policy, or memory-selection behavior; applications must define their own records and retrieval logic.

The graph language is a bounded subset rather than full SQL/PGQ; vector retrieval is exact-only in this release, and the clustered/indexed route is disabled. The documented design envelope is 10K–1M rows per database with sparse graphs and bounded depth, not a guarantee for every workload.

The repository explicitly excludes general multi-tenant orchestration, Python and TypeScript bindings, and built-in cross-tenant isolation. ACL/context controls are opt-in and deployment boundaries remain material.

Logical deletion, retention, version cleanup, file compaction, and backup recovery are distinct. Documentation does not promise secure forensic erasure or that a reclaimed logical row immediately reduces file size.

This review inspected selected official README, architecture, capability, query-language, sync, and engine sources at the current dev head. It did not audit every crate, adapter, or deployment; no checkout was available through the read-only command environment, so source was inspected on official SHA-pinned GitHub pages. No runtime, tests, or benchmarks were run.
